questions.q: What specific physical detail does the author use in the opening paragraph to emphasize the height and danger of the ledge where the young seagull stands?
questions.a: The author describes "a sheer drop to the sea" and "the great expanse of sea stretching down beneath" to establish vertigo-inducing height. A wrong answer (e.g., "the nest was high" or "the wind was strong") reveals the student is summarizing rather than citing precise textual imagery, which loses marks in CBSE answer writing where specific evidence is required.

questions.q: Why does the young seagull pretend to fall asleep when his parents and siblings are watching him?
questions.a: He pretends to sleep to avoid facing their expectations and his own shame, masking his paralysis with feigned indifference. A wrong answer like "he was tired" shows the student misses the psychological defense mechanism — a common board exam trap where literal reading replaces inference about character motivation.

questions.q: Identify two sensory details the author uses to describe the mother seagull's flight with the piece of fish, and explain how each detail intensifies the young seagull's desperation.
questions.a: 1) Visual: "tearing at a piece of fish" — shows food being consumed nearby. 2) Auditory: "screaming" — the mother's call mocks his hunger. Together they transform abstract hunger into visceral torture. A wrong answer listing only "she flew with fish" without sensory analysis fails the "explain how" requirement of CBSE 3-mark questions.

questions.q: Compare the father's and mother's methods of encouraging the young seagull. Which method is more effective in this part of the story, and why?
questions.a: The father uses scolding ("taunting him with his cowardice") and demonstration (flying with siblings); the mother uses strategic temptation (flying close with food but not giving it). The mother's method works because it exploits the primal drive of hunger, while shame-based tactics only deepen paralysis. A wrong answer claiming both are equally effective ignores the narrative climax where only the mother's action triggers the dive.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The young seagull's fear is entirely irrational because flying is his natural instinct." Defend or refute using evidence from the text.
questions.a: Refute. The text shows instinct alone is insufficient — he feels "certain that his wings would never support him" despite watching siblings fly. Fear is rational when past failure (implied by "he had been afraid to fly with them") combines with physiological vertigo. A wrong answer agreeing with the statement overlooks the text's emphasis on psychological barriers overriding instinct — a nuance CBSE expects in evaluation questions.

questions.q: Write a 4-line internal monologue for the young seagull at the moment he sees the fish in his mother's beak, capturing the conflict between fear and hunger.
questions.a: Example: "The fish glints — life itself / My wings freeze, the ledge feels wide / Hunger screams louder than the void / One lunge, or die here waiting." A poor answer writes generic fear ("I am scared") without the specific tension of the fish as catalyst, showing inability to synthesize character voice with plot turning point.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The young seagull's fear of flying represents the universal ______ barrier of confronting the unknown, where innate instinct conflicts with learned apprehension, and overcoming it requires an external catalyst (hunger) combined with internal realization of capability.
Fill in the blank: Imagine ______ at the edge of a high diving board for the first time — your legs shake, your heart races, and every instinct screams to step back.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain, using textual evidence, how the author portrays the seagull's fear through sensory details and internal monologue, and can articulate the turning point where fear begins to shift toward action.
